I drift off into a world of my own
Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

vignette: Tunde was forty-two when the coordinated bombing shattered the morning routine at the federal courthouse annex. He had been in the second-floor atrium processing property records when the first pressure wave threw him against the oak circulation desk. Through the acrid smoke, he watched a man in a heavy wool coat collapse, his leather briefcase cracking open to spill ledgers and envelopes across the tiled floor. When the second explosion rolled through the stairwell, the glass facade spiderwebbed, and the air turned to a sharp, metallic static. Tunde dragged himself toward the emergency exit, his palms slick, his ears ringing as he guided a disoriented patron toward the street. In those minutes, the world narrowed to the smell of scorched insulation, the sound of groaning steel, and the chilling realization that a routine public space could be turned into a killing ground. When Tunde returned to his duties at the municipal library, his internal landscape shifted in tandem with his physical recovery. The memories of that morning remained entirely intact, not as hazy impressions but as precise, unblinking scenes. He could recall the exact scuff marks on the marble steps, the pattern of the shattered glass, the way the briefcase had skidded across the tile. His mind would press replay, the sequence unspooling in his head like a film that would not be paused. Often, a sudden sound—a metal cart rolling into a book drop, a patron’s sudden cough, the heavy thud of a delivery door—would hijack his attention, and for a breathless moment, he was back in that marble lobby, certain the ceiling was about to give way. Alongside these unwavering memories, his attention kept catching on specific dates and discussions. As the anniversary of the event approached, Tunde found his shoulders drawing inward weeks in advance, a quiet, mechanical dread that turned the calendar into a countdown. He also noticed how certain conversation topics, especially those drifting toward public infrastructure, emergency protocols, or unexplained disruptions in civic life, made the air in a room feel suddenly thin. He would listen with a tight jaw, his thoughts carefully still. Parallel to these intrusions, other patterns settled into his daily rhythm. Tunde stopped attending the library’s autumn book fairs and holiday readings. He told himself it was because he preferred solitude, but the reality was simpler: he could not bear situations that might make him feel happy or hopeful. Joy felt like a precarious thing, a fragile state that he worried he had no right to occupy. When the weight of the present grew too sharp, he learned to drift off into a world of his own, letting his gaze soften on the spines of stacked books while his mind wandered to quiet, unfamiliar landscapes. He also began to avoid crowds. Shopping centers, community forums, and even the busy lunch hours at the library felt like spaces he had to navigate with his shoulders braced. He would keep to the outer edges of aisles, his eyes tracking the main doors, counting patrons rather than engaging with them. The consequences of these patterns were concrete. At work, Tunde requested a permanent shift change to early mornings, when the reading rooms were nearly empty. He withdrew from the library’s public lecture series, citing fatigue, though his wife, Amara, noticed how his hands would tremble when she mentioned the annual neighborhood festival they used to attend together. He began leaving the house through the side gate, taking longer routes to the staff entrance, telling himself it was to avoid traffic. He knew it was to keep his distance from the surge of people, from the unpredictable movements that filled a room with unpredictable noise. His work grew meticulous but isolated. He filed, reshelved, and processed returns with careful precision, never engaging in the longer conversations with regulars that once filled his afternoons with warmth. Now, at seventy-eight, Tunde sits in the waiting room of a community mental health clinic, his hands folded over his knees. He came because Amara gently insisted that the silence between them had grown too heavy, that the way he flinched at sirens and checked exit signs in restaurants was costing him what little peace remained. He tells himself he is not looking for a cure, only a way to make the memories stop dictating his hours. What he fears most is losing the careful distance he has built, that if he lets his guard down, the past will rush back and take the last fragile years he has left. What he hopes for, quietly, is simply to walk through a crowded room without counting the doors, to sit in a sunlit café and let himself feel the day as it is, rather than as it was.
